query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale high-entropy-alloy (HEA) multilayer coatings, sustained loading induces progressive plastic deformation primarily via the accumulation and gradual motion of edge dislocations that are slowed and locally pinned by compositional fluctuations and resulting lattice distortions at the layer interfaces. Over time, these pinned dislocation segments (forming wavy dislocation lines) facilitate interface‐mediated strain relaxation and localized plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating with alternating FCC and BCC HEA layers exhibiting coherent or semi-coherent interfaces, with inherent compositional complexity and associated lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Apply a sustained load (creep conditions) under controlled temperature conditions that retain the nanoscale multilayer structure.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at room or moderately elevated temperatures (to avoid diffusion-induced degradation) with a constant stress level set within the elastic-plastic transition regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The alternating layers and their coherent interfaces that magnify the effects of lattice distortion from compositional fluctuations, leading to localized pinning of edge dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The random distribution of multiple elements in the HEA layers creates severe lattice distortion that deflects the cores of predominantly <111>{110} edge dislocations. Under sustained loading, these dislocations become locally pinned at the interfaces due to the compositional and crystallographic mismatches, leading to z-direction (through-thickness) progressive accumulation and activation of plastic flow along the interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial undeformed multilayer state, creep tests would show an increasing density of pinned and wavy edge dislocations particularly near layer boundaries, accompanied by a measurable progressive plastic strain and local interface shear. This effect is predicted to be more pronounced in multilayers with a higher degree of compositional fluctuation.
generation.baseline: Pre-sustained-loading state with minimal dislocation accumulation and a uniform layered structure as formed during deposition.
generation.boundary: Observations apply only if the nanoscale multilayer structure is maintained without significant interdiffusion or interface decohesion (i.e., below temperatures where diffusion processes become dominant) and for applied stresses within the range that do not cause catastrophic failure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of interface-pinning versus intra-layer dislocation motion is uncertain, and the influence of potential differences between FCC and BCC layer behaviors on dislocation dynamics remains to be fully delineated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoscale HEA multilayer coatings that are identical except for controlled variations in interface quality (e.g., one with highly coherent interfaces and one with intentionally reduced interface coherence). Subject both sets to identical sustained stress (creep) tests at temperatures low enough to retain the layered microstructure yet high enough to activate dislocation mobility. Use high-resolution TEM and in situ diffraction techniques to map dislocation structures and quantify plastic strain evolution.
measurements: TEM imaging of dislocation pile-up and interface structure before and after creep.
Quantitative analysis of creep strain rates over time.
Mapping of local lattice distortions and interface shear via high-resolution diffraction or similar techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If sustained loading does not result in a significantly higher density of pinned/wavy edge dislocations at the layer interfaces (compared to the baseline and relative to the control with altered interface quality) or if the progressive plastic strain is not correlated with such interfacial dislocation accumulation, then the hypothesis that interface-mediated dislocation pinning governs the progressive plastic deformation would be falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
